title: Psalm 124: If the LORD Had Not Been on Our Side
summary: Israel is invited to say aloud what would have happened if the LORD had not been on its side: enemies would have swallowed the nation alive, and floodwaters would have swept it away. Instead the people praise God, who did not hand them over as prey, and who tore the net so they escaped like a bird from a trap. Their help, they confess, is in the name of the Maker of heaven and earth.
story: Psalm 123 ended with the people still waiting for mercy under the scorn of the proud. Psalm 124 answers from memory: God has rescued before, and his people can say so. It is the Songs of Ascents' first full thanksgiving, and it looks back on a danger already past. Its final line nearly repeats Psalm 121:2, where a single pilgrim said his help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth; here the whole community says it together. What one traveler confessed on the road becomes the song of a nation that has come through.
historical:
The heading reads “A song of ascents. Of David.” As with other psalms in this collection, the attribution to David is not found in every ancient manuscript and translation, and the Hebrew phrase can mean by, for, or in the manner of David. Those who read it as Davidic point to the many enemies David faced, from the Philistines to Absalom's revolt, and the deliverances he celebrated in other psalms. Many scholars instead read Psalm 124 as a later communal thanksgiving, pointing to Hebrew forms that are more common in late biblical Hebrew, and date it to the period after the exile.

The psalm names no enemy and no battle. Some interpreters connect it with a particular rescue, such as Jerusalem's deliverance from the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 BC (2 Kings 18-19), or with the return from Babylon. Others think its generality is deliberate: it is a liturgy for remembering all of God's rescues, from the exodus onward, so that any generation could sing it about its own deliverance.
cultural:
Two pictures of danger dominate the psalm, and both were vivid to ancient Israel. The first is flood. The land of Israel has wadis, dry stream beds that fill without warning when winter rain falls on the hills, and a sudden torrent can sweep away a traveler or a flock. Beyond that everyday danger, raging waters were a common ancient picture of chaos and death, the power God tamed at creation and split at the Red Sea. Being “swallowed alive” recalls the earth opening under Korah and his followers in the wilderness (Numbers 16:30-33) and the grave pictured as a mouth that devours.

The second picture is the bird trap. Fowlers caught small birds for food with nets and spring snares, and Israel's poets often used the image for sudden, hidden danger (Proverbs 7:23; Ecclesiastes 9:12). A bird in a snare cannot free itself; it escapes only if the snare breaks. That is the point of verse 7: the net was torn, and the bird was gone. The escape is not the bird's doing.
literary: Psalm 124 is a communal thanksgiving with a liturgical frame. The words “let Israel now declare” in verse 1 are a leader's call for the congregation to respond, the same formula found in Psalm 129:1 and Psalm 118:2. The first five verses are one long conditional sentence: if not for the LORD (verses 1-2), then (Hebrew azay, three times in verses 3-5) disaster. The repeated then builds pressure like rising water, and the images climb from anger to swallowing to flood to torrent to raging waters. Verse 6 breaks the tension with praise, and verse 7 changes the picture from drowning to a trapped bird, with a stair-step repetition of snare and escape. Verse 8 closes with a confession that sums up the whole.

outline.t: If the LORD had not been on our side
What would have happened: swallowed and swept away
Praise for rescue: not prey, but an escaped bird
Our help is in the name of the LORD

doctrines.note: Deliverance in this psalm is entirely God's act. The people do not fight their way out; the net is torn and they slip away. The whole song is built on the assumption that without the LORD they would have been lost.
The psalm teaches Israel to read its history by imagining the alternative: if not for the LORD. Remembering what did not happen becomes a way of seeing God's hidden protection.
The closing confession grounds help in God's identity as “the Maker of heaven and earth.” The one who made the waters can hold them back.

words.note: Lule, if not, unless. It opens the psalm twice and sets its whole shape: a contrary-to-fact condition, a way of saying what would have been. Memory of grace often works this way, by seeing how close disaster came.

Malat, to escape or slip away. It is used for fleeing danger, like David slipping away from Saul (1 Samuel 19:10-12). In verse 7 it appears twice, once for the bird's escape and once for the people's, with the torn net between them. The escape is real, but the verb in context credits God for making it possible.

Pach, snare or trap. It was a fowler's device, often a net or spring trap that snapped shut. In the Old Testament it becomes a word for any hidden danger laid for someone (Psalm 91:3 promises rescue from the fowler's snare). Here the snare is broken, not avoided.

Ezer, help. The same word the lone pilgrim used in Psalm 121:1-2, now spoken by the whole people. Many Reformed churches have long opened worship with this verse as a call to worship, a confession that everything that follows depends on God's help.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 124, but its logic appears in Paul's great question: if God is for us, who can be against us? (Romans 8:31). The psalm's pictures of being swallowed and overwhelmed by waters are the Old Testament's pictures of death, and the church confesses that in Christ's resurrection God did for him, and through him for his people, what the psalm describes. Peter's sermon at Pentecost says God raised Jesus because it was impossible for death to keep its hold on him (Acts 2:24). Jesus also spoke of himself as protecting his own in the hour of danger, asking that his disciples be allowed to go free when he was arrested (John 18:8-9). The link is thematic and typological: the rescues Israel remembered in this psalm become a pattern that finds its deepest expression at the empty tomb.
questions: Try the psalm's exercise: finish the sentence, if the LORD had not been on my side, then... What did you escape that you rarely think about?
The bird in verse 7 does nothing to escape except fly when the net tears. How does that picture challenge the way you think about your own rescues?
Why might it matter that the community says this psalm together rather than each person alone?
